checkpoints: `LIKE '%X%'` with a leading wildcard cannot use a B-tree, since a B-tree only optimizes prefix/range lookups — Postgres is forced into a full-table scan of every row, O(N) cost, e.g. 5-10 seconds on a ~1M-row catalog.
The result set from that scan carries no relevance order at all.
Elasticsearch runs an analyzer that turns each text field into terms: tokenize, lowercase, drop stopwords, stem.
ES builds an inverted index mapping every term to a posting list holding the ids of every document containing that term.
At query time ES looks up posting lists at near O(1) per term instead of scanning the whole table, answering in tens of milliseconds even for 1M documents.
Beyond speed, ES adds relevance ranking via `_score` under the BM25 formula.
ES also adds typo tolerance via `fuzziness: "AUTO"`, phrase matching, and faceted aggregation in the same query.
This isn't a faster version of the same substring scan — it's a different data model, a reverse dictionary from term to documents, not a sequentially scanned table.
`LIKE 'mac%'` can use a B-tree index, but every keystroke still costs its own query to disk.
A Trie is O(k) and runs entirely in RAM, independent of N — a 3-character prefix over 1 million words costs roughly 3 pointer hops.
The path from the root IS the prefix; the node you land on is the root of the subtree holding every possible completion.
Frequency/ranking score is stored right on the word's terminal node.
A single DFS over that subtree both collects candidates and already has the scores to rank the top-K, with no secondary lookup.
A missed prefix returns empty right at the first unmatched character (no matching child node), never scanning the whole dictionary.
In exchange for an in-memory character tree, you get O(k) lookup with ranking baked directly into the structure itself.

A Trie that inserts and looks up words via raw `for (const char of word)` without lowercasing treats `MacBook`, `macbook`, and `MAC` as three distinct character sequences, so each variant walks into its own branch of `children` instead of converging on one node.

Because each case variant lives in a separate branch, the frequency counter accumulates separately per branch instead of summing across all inserts of the same logical word — the genuinely popular term ends up looking less popular than its own case variants and ranks below them.

Iterating a string by codepoint (`for...of`) builds the tree structure correctly, but it does not guarantee that visually and semantically identical characters produce the same codepoint sequence — an accented character typed in decomposed form (NFD: base letter plus a separate combining mark) and in composed form (NFC: a single codepoint) are different sequences, so they take different paths through the Trie even though a user reads them as the same word.

This Unicode split is a genuine internationalization bug rather than a hypothetical edge case: different keyboards, input methods, and operating systems can produce NFD or NFC for the same Vietnamese word such as `cà phê`, so real user traffic can hit the split without any malformed input.

The correct fix is to normalize on both the write path and the read path with the same transformation — lowercase and `.normalize('NFC')` applied before `insert` walks the word and before `suggest` walks the prefix — because normalizing only one of the two functions still leaves the data written and the query read following different conventions, so lookups fail to find data that was actually inserted.

The bug passed code review because the team's seed data was entirely ASCII and already lowercase, so the test suite never exercised a mixed-case branch or an accented character; the defect only becomes visible once real traffic contains case variation or accented text.

A correctness test for this fix should insert the same logical word multiple times using different case variants and both NFD and NFC forms, then assert that `suggest` returns exactly one entry for that word with a frequency equal to the sum of every insert, ranked according to that combined total.

In a per-item indexing loop, the dominant cost is not the write work itself but the N separate HTTP round-trips to Elasticsearch — 50,000 products means 50,000 individual requests, each paying its own network latency and per-request overhead, and that overhead multiplied by 50,000 is where the minutes actually go.

The Bulk API collapses many individual `index()` calls into one HTTP request: build a flat `operations` array where each document is preceded by its own meta line, `{ index: { _index, _id } }`, followed by the document body, then send it in a single `es.bulk({ operations })` call.

Batching roughly 2,000-5,000 documents (or capping around a few MB) per bulk call turns 50,000 round-trips into on the order of 10-25 requests, which is exactly where the 10-100x throughput gain comes from — Elasticsearch is not writing any faster, the code is just paying the round-trip cost far fewer times.

Keeping `refresh: false` (the async default) during a backfill avoids forcing a synchronous segment refresh on every batch, which would throttle throughput just to buy a read-after-write guarantee a bulk backfill rarely needs.

A bulk response can return success at the HTTP level while individual items inside it still fail, so the response's `errors` boolean must be checked and `items` walked to find and retry only the specific documents that failed, instead of assuming the whole batch succeeded.

Correctness after switching to bulk writes is confirmed by comparing the final document count in the target index against the source count, which catches documents silently dropped by an unnoticed partial failure.

The claimed speed-up is verified empirically, not assumed, by timing the batched version against the original per-item loop on the same 50,000-product dataset and confirming the wall-clock time drops by an order of magnitude.

Diagnosing before proposing a fix means naming "N network round-trips" explicitly as the bottleneck rather than a vague "the loop is slow" — it is the round-trip count, not the Elasticsearch indexing engine, that explains the multi-minute runtime.

The `persistState` method calls `this.trie.serialize()` on the entire tree and writes it under one Redis key (`STATE_KEY`) inside every `recordSearch` call, so a single recorded query costs O(tree size), not O(word length).

At small scale this per-call whole-tree serialization is invisible, but at millions of nodes every recorded query re-serializes and rewrites a multi-megabyte JSON blob, so write latency and Redis payload size scale with total dictionary size rather than with the term just recorded.
The in-memory Trie never evicts anything, so long-tail one-off searches accumulate as permanent nodes and memory grows unbounded in lockstep with the write cost.

Debouncing or batching `persistState` — using a dirty flag flushed on a timer or after N calls instead of synchronously inside `recordSearch` — turns per-query writes into periodic snapshots, at the cost of losing the last few seconds of records on an unclean crash.

Replacing the whole-tree snapshot with a Redis-native structure, such as a per-prefix ZSET updated via `ZINCRBY` on write and read with `ZREVRANGE ... WITHSCORES`, makes each recorded query touch only the sub-prefixes it belongs to, turning the write into an incremental update instead of a whole-tree rewrite.

Bounding memory is a separate fix from bounding write cost: capping a minimum hit frequency and dropping entries below it on a periodic sweep, TTL-expiring long-tail keys, or compressing the in-memory Trie into a Radix tree that collapses single-child chains into one node.

Moving state into per-prefix ZSETs shifts sorting work into Redis and adds one write per matching sub-prefix instead of one whole-tree write per query, so the choice between debouncing and the ZSET redesign follows the durability/latency budget rather than being a universally 'better' option.

The `suggest` read path only walks the in-memory Trie and never touches `persistState` or Redis, so any fix to the write path should leave read latency unaffected — verified with a before/after load test that grows the dictionary and checks that Redis write payload size and `suggest` p99 flatten instead of climbing with tree size.
States that Debezium picks up the new column automatically from the Postgres WAL, with no code or config change required on the source side.
Correctly identifies Elasticsearch — not Postgres/Debezium — as the actual point where this pipeline can break.
States that a strict/explicit ES mapping rejects events carrying the unfamiliar `warranty_months` field outright.
States that careless dynamic mapping risks ES guessing the wrong type for the field (e.g., indexing a number as `text`).
Names the concrete downstream consequence of that mistyping: range queries and aggregations on the field later break.
States the explicit ordering contract: deploy/update the ES mapping for `warranty_months` BEFORE running the Postgres `ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN` migration.

Proposes a proactive safeguard beyond ordering alone: alert on Debezium's `schema-changes` topic so the team learns of a source schema change immediately, instead of discovering it via a stream of ES indexing failures.
Define a `SuggestionSource` contract — `record(query)` and `suggest(prefix, limit) → ranked [{word, score}]` — as the only thing a caller ever talks to.
The contract owns prefix semantics, the ranked top-K shape, and normalization (case-folding, NFC), so every implementation agrees on what a prefix means before comparing characters.
Everything else stays hidden inside each implementation: the Trie's O(k) walk + DFS + in-process sort, the Redis ZSET's `ZINCRBY`/`ZREVRANGE`, and the ES completion suggester's FST-based traversal.
A caller switching from one backing implementation to another should not need to change anything beyond which class it constructs.
The in-memory Trie wins on raw single-node latency but has no way to share its learned frequencies across replicas — each instance is its own island.

The per-prefix Redis ZSET shares state across replicas and lets Redis itself do the sorting on `ZREVRANGE` (no fetch-then-sort), at the cost of heavier writes since recording one query bumps a ZSET member for every sub-prefix of that word.

The Elasticsearch completion suggester is only worth it when you already run ES infrastructure and specifically need multi-language tokenizers or fuzzy/typo-tolerant matching — not just to get O(k) prefix lookup you already have in a Trie.

The guarantees differ across implementations despite the identical interface — Trie is strongly consistent within one process but dies with it, ZSET is only as consistent as Redis's replication, ES suggester trails by CDC/indexing lag — and this must be documented on the contract, not assumed uniform.

Dual-write is two non-atomic commits: PostgreSQL can succeed while the Elasticsearch call fails (or vice versa), causing permanent divergence with no rollback, because no single transaction can span two different systems.
A transactional outbox only solves half the problem: it makes the intent to emit an event atomic within one transaction on one DB.
The app code still has to remember to emit that event on every write path — missing one endpoint, running raw SQL directly, or running a migration bypasses the outbox completely.
CDC changes WHERE the change is captured: Debezium tails the PostgreSQL WAL directly instead of capturing it at scattered app call-sites.

The WAL is the single source of truth every transaction writes into whether it goes through the app or not, so CDC captures every commit — including manual raw SQL or migrations — with no app-side emit needed.
Adding a new downstream consumer later (a cache, a data warehouse) is just adding a new consumer reading the same Kafka topic, with no change to the producer.
The price of CDC is a 4-hop pipeline (WAL flush → Debezium reads → Kafka publishes → consumer indexes) and a few seconds of eventual-consistency lag instead of instant consistency.
Key principle: capture the change at the transaction log, not at scattered call-sites throughout the app code.
`text` fields are tokenized/lowercased/stopword-dropped/stemmed by an analyzer and placed into the inverted index — full-text searchable, but not aggregatable.
`keyword` fields are stored as-is with no tokenizing — exact match, `term` filter, and aggregation work, but not full-text search.
`name` → `text`, because the search requirement needs term-by-term matching that stays tolerant of the exact query wording (e.g. "macbook pro").
`category` → `keyword`, because the facet sidebar's counts need a `terms` aggregation, which only works on an untokenized field.
`brand` → `keyword`, because the requirement needs an exact filter match plus a stable A→Z sort on the original string.

If `category` is mistakenly mapped as `text`, the `terms` aggregation counts wrong — by individual term after tokenizing, or fails with a fielddata error — instead of counting by the real category group, producing meaningless facet numbers.

When a field needs both full-text search and exact aggregate/sort (like `name`), declare a multi-field — e.g. `name: { type: "text", fields: { keyword: { type: "keyword" } } }` — so search goes through `name` while aggregation and exact sort go through `name.keyword`.
Operating principle: declare the mapping explicitly up front rather than letting dynamic mapping guess, to avoid schema drift once real data exists.
This behavior is not a bug — it is inherent to the CDC → Elasticsearch pipeline's architecture.

The latency comes from 4 hops — WAL flush in PostgreSQL, Debezium reading via `pgoutput`, publishing to Kafka, and the consumer indexing into Elasticsearch — each adding a bit of delay so ES always trails PG by a few seconds.
Key distinction: PostgreSQL is the source of truth, while Elasticsearch is only a derived view kept in sync through CDC.
Any flow that needs read-your-writes, such as the screen where the user just edited the listing, must read from PostgreSQL, not from Elasticsearch.
Flows like browsing, general search, or facet filtering tolerate the few-second lag fine since they never expect every change reflected instantly.

Mitigation: after saving, fetch the listing's detail back from PG (or apply an optimistic update on the client) instead of waiting for ES to catch up, optionally with a small "re-indexing..." hint for transparency.

In exchange for that short lag window, the system gains real decoupling and durability — Kafka retains every event so a crashed consumer can replay without data loss, and adding a new downstream only needs a new consumer on the same topic with no producer change.
Principle: design flows around eventual consistency — that is the price of a decoupled pipeline, not a defect to patch.
